title: Requirements and tradeoffs
summary: Separate actions from quality goals. Compare two library plans, keep the rules that must hold, and write down a useful tradeoff.
introduction: Two school bags can both carry books. One is lighter; another has more pockets. Choosing between them depends on what you need. App designs also involve choices like these.
learningObjectives: Identify a rule that must always hold
Explain the benefit and cost of a design choice

blocks.text: A **requirement** says what the system needs to do or how well it needs to work. An action, such as searching for a book, is a functional requirement. A quality goal says how fast, reliable, or easy to use that action should be.
A **constraint** is a limit we must work within, such as a small budget or a team of two people. A **tradeoff** is a choice where gaining one benefit may cost something else.
Some rules protect the meaning of the data. For example, one physical library copy must not have two active loans at once. We cannot quietly break this rule just to make a busy request finish faster.
Use made-up planning units when comparing cost in this lesson. The values below are examples, not real cloud prices.

rows: 95 of 100 searches under 2 seconds at expected peak load
At most one active loan per copy
Stay within 20 planning units per month
blocks.caption: Four different kinds of planning statements

items: Write the action: a learner reserves an available book copy.
Write the rule: a copy can have only one active reservation.
Write the speed goal: 95 of 100 searches should finish within 2 seconds at the expected busy time.
Compare a small plan and a larger plan against the same needs. Choose the smallest one that can meet them.
Record the reason and what new evidence would make you change the choice.

blocks.code:
Budget limit: 20 planning units per month
Plan A: one app, one database, cost 10 units
Plan B: two apps, database copies, cost 35 units
First choice: Plan A, if testing meets the speed goal
Accepted limit: app maintenance may pause the service
Revisit when: measured demand or uptime needs grow
blocks.title: Requirements and tradeoffs example

blocks.text: Plan A fits the example budget. Plan B may handle some failures better, but it costs more and needs more care. More app copies alone do not remove every failure; the database and network still matter.
A decision record is a short note explaining the choice, reason, and known limits. It helps the next person understand the plan instead of guessing why it looks that way.
Requirements can conflict. If the school needs uninterrupted access but cannot fund the needed design, explain the conflict and ask which goal can change. Do not pretend all goals are met.
Avoid words such as fast or reliable on their own. Say which action is timed, at what expected demand, and how success will be counted.

items: Suppose the budget rises to 40 units. Does that prove Plan B is the best choice?
No. It makes Plan B affordable, but you still need a reason to pay for it. Compare the required uptime, measured load, and extra work needed to run it.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not treat every nice idea as a must-have rule. Write what is required now and what can wait until a real need appears.
